categoryBlurb: The plate around the plate — crackly roast potatoes, a bowl of greens with dressing you made yourself, bread pulled out of the oven at the last minute. These are the things people actually fight over at the table.

recipes.title: Garlic Mashed Potatoes
recipes.blurb: Silky, buttery, and sweet with whole garlic cloves that simmered right alongside the potatoes. Once you mash them this way you will not go back to the boxed kind.

items: 3 lb (1.35 kg) Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 2-inch (5 cm) chunks
8 large garlic cloves, peeled and left whole
1 tbsp (18 g) kosher salt, for the cooking water
Cold water to cover by 1 inch (2.5 cm), about 3 qt (2.8 L)
8 tbsp (113 g) unsalted butter, cut into 8 pieces
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 tbsp (6 g) chopped fresh chives, for serving

instructions.title: Cut the potatoes evenly
instructions.text: Peel the potatoes and cut them into chunks about 2 inches (5 cm) across, keeping the pieces as close to the same size as you can. Uneven pieces are the number one cause of gummy mash, because the small ones blow apart and turn waterlogged while you wait for the big ones. Drop the cut pieces straight into the pot so they do not sit out and oxidize.

instructions.title: Start them in cold water
instructions.text: Put the potatoes and the 8 whole garlic cloves in a large pot and cover with cold water by about 1 inch (2.5 cm). Starting cold lets the outside and the inside come up to temperature together, so the edges do not turn to mush before the centers cook. If you drop potatoes into already-boiling water you get a ragged, watery exterior every time.

instructions.title: Salt the water properly
instructions.text: Add 1 tablespoon (18 g) of kosher salt to the pot and stir. Potatoes are starchy and bland and they will only be seasoned all the way through if they cook in seasoned water — salting at the end never catches up. The water should taste noticeably salty, a little less than seawater.

instructions.title: Simmer, do not boil hard
instructions.text: Bring the pot to a boil over high heat, then drop it to medium-low so the water moves at a lazy simmer with just a few bubbles breaking the surface. Cook for 15 to 20 minutes, until the tip of a paring knife slides into a chunk and the piece falls off the blade with no resistance. A hard rolling boil knocks the potatoes against each other and washes starch into the water, which costs you creaminess.

instructions.title: Warm the dairy, soften the butter
instructions.text: While the potatoes cook, put the 1 cup (240 ml) milk and the 1/2 cup (120 ml) cream in a small saucepan over low heat until steaming but not simmering, about 5 minutes, then pull it off the burner. Leave the 8 tablespoons (113 g) of cut-up butter on the counter so it is soft but not melted — it goes in on its own, before the liquid. Cold dairy hitting hot potatoes seizes the starch and makes the mash stiff and pasty, while warm dairy gets absorbed instead. That is most of the difference between home mash and restaurant mash.

instructions.title: Drain and dry them out
instructions.text: Drain the potatoes and garlic in a colander, then tip them back into the empty hot pot and set it over low heat for 1 to 2 minutes. Shake the pot gently and you will see steam rising off the surface as the last of the water evaporates. Drier potatoes drink up more butter, and butter is the whole point.

instructions.title: Rice them while hot
instructions.text: Press the hot potatoes and the softened garlic cloves through a potato ricer or a food mill back into the pot. If you do not own one, use a hand masher and stop the second the lumps are gone. Never use a blender, food processor, or hand mixer on high — they rupture the starch cells and turn potatoes into wallpaper paste in about ten seconds.

instructions.title: Butter first, then dairy
instructions.text: Add all 8 tablespoons (113 g) of the softened butter to the hot riced potatoes and fold with a flexible spatula until it has completely disappeared. Only then add the warm milk and cream, in three additions, stirring gently after each one and stopping when the mash is as loose as you like it. Going fat-first coats the starch granules in butter so they cannot soak up the liquid and swell into glue — do it in the other order and you get wallpaper paste. Stop stirring as soon as everything is combined and glossy, because every extra stroke works more starch loose.

instructions.title: Season and adjust
instructions.text: Stir in 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt and the 1/4 teaspoon white pepper, then taste. Potatoes need more salt than you think, so add another 1/4 teaspoon at a time until the flavor snaps into focus rather than tasting flat. If the mash is thicker than you like, loosen it with warm milk 2 tablespoons (30 ml) at a time.

instructions.title: Hold and serve warm
instructions.text: Serve within 20 minutes, or keep the mash warm in a heatproof bowl set over a pot of barely simmering water with a lid on, stirring once every 15 minutes. Scatter the chives over the top just before it hits the table so they stay green. Mashed potatoes should be served hot, above 150°F (66°C), or the butter stiffens and the texture goes waxy.

tips: Yukon Golds are the sweet spot — waxy enough to stay creamy, starchy enough to fluff. Russets make a fluffier, drier mash; red potatoes turn gluey and are worth skipping here.
Make ahead: mash up to 2 days early, cool, and refrigerate. Reheat in a covered baking dish at 350°F (175°C) for 30 minutes with an extra 1/4 cup (60 ml) of warm milk stirred in.
For a deeper, sweeter garlic flavor, roast a whole head at 400°F (200°C) for 40 minutes and squeeze the cloves in at the end instead of boiling them.
If the mash goes gluey, it cannot be fixed — but you can spread it in a buttered dish, top with cheese, and bake it into a potato casserole nobody will question.
Leftovers make excellent potato cakes: mix in an egg, form patties, and pan-fry in butter over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side.
recipes.keyTemp: Potatoes are done when a knife meets no resistance, around 210°F (99°C) internal. Serve above 150°F (66°C) so the butter stays emulsified and the mash stays silky.
recipes.pairing: The natural partner to roast chicken, meatloaf, or any braise with gravy — pour a glass of unoaked Chardonnay or a soft red.

recipes.title: Extra Crispy Roast Potatoes
recipes.blurb: Parboiled, roughed up until the edges go fuzzy, then roasted in hot fat until they shatter. The outside is glass and the inside is cloud, and there are never enough of them.

items: 4 lb (1.8 kg) Yukon Gold or russet potatoes, peeled and cut into 2-inch (5 cm) chunks
2 tbsp (36 g) kosher salt, for the water
5 tbsp (75 ml) olive oil, duck fat, or beef tallow
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh parsley, for serving

instructions.title: Heat the oven and the fat
instructions.text: Set a rack in the center of the oven and heat it to 450°F (230°C). Pour the 5 tablespoons (75 ml) of fat onto a heavy rimmed sheet pan and slide it into the oven while it preheats. Potatoes hitting an already-screaming-hot pan of fat start crisping instantly instead of slowly absorbing cold oil and going greasy.

instructions.title: Cut for maximum surface
instructions.text: Cut the potatoes into chunks roughly 2 inches (5 cm) across, aiming for pieces with several flat faces rather than smooth rounds. Every flat face is a future crispy plane, and every sharp corner is a future crunchy bit. Halve small potatoes and quarter large ones so they all cook at the same rate.

instructions.title: Build the alkaline water
instructions.text: Put the potatoes in a large pot with 3 quarts (2.8 L) of cold water, 2 tablespoons (36 g) kosher salt, and the 1/2 teaspoon baking soda. The baking soda makes the water alkaline, which breaks down pectin on the outside of each piece and creates the starchy slurry that turns into the crust. It is one half teaspoon and it is the entire trick.

instructions.title: Parboil until the edges give
instructions.text: Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a strong simmer and cook for 10 minutes, until a knife slides into a chunk easily but the piece still holds its shape. Do not stir once they are tender or you will break them apart. If they are falling apart at 8 minutes, pull them immediately — different potatoes cook at different speeds.

instructions.title: Drain and steam dry
instructions.text: Drain the potatoes in a colander and let them sit for 2 full minutes, shaking once, until the steam stops pouring off and the surfaces look dull and dry. Surface water has to boil away before browning can start, so every second here is a second of crisping you buy back. Dry potatoes also stop the hot fat from spitting at you.

instructions.title: Rough them up
instructions.text: Tip the potatoes back into the empty pot, add the 1 teaspoon salt and the black pepper, and shake the pot hard 8 to 10 times with the lid on. The surfaces should go visibly fuzzy and coated in a pale starchy paste. That mashed-up exterior is what fries into the craggy shell — a smooth potato roasts smooth and disappointing.

instructions.title: Get them into the hot fat
instructions.text: Pull the sheet pan out carefully — the fat will be shimmering and may wisp slightly. Tip the potatoes on, then use tongs to turn each one so all sides are coated, and spread them out so no two pieces touch. Crowding traps steam and steamed potatoes never crisp, so use two pans if yours looks tight.

instructions.title: Roast without touching
instructions.text: Roast for 25 minutes without opening the door. The bottoms need uninterrupted contact with the hot pan to set a crust, and every peek drops the oven temperature by 25 to 50 degrees. You should hear a steady sizzle when you finally open it, not silence and not violent spitting.

instructions.title: Flip and add aromatics
instructions.text: Slide a thin metal spatula under each potato and flip it, scraping up any crust that wants to stick to the pan. Tuck the crushed garlic cloves and rosemary sprigs in among the potatoes now, not earlier — 45 minutes at 450°F (230°C) would turn them black and bitter. Return the pan to the oven.

instructions.title: Finish to deep gold
instructions.text: Roast another 20 to 30 minutes, flipping once more at the halfway point, until the potatoes are deep golden brown and sound hollow and hard when you tap them with tongs. Pale potatoes are undercooked potatoes — push them further than feels comfortable. The interior should read about 210°F (99°C) and be completely fluffy.

instructions.title: Salt and serve immediately
instructions.text: Transfer to a warm serving bowl, hit them with a pinch more salt while the surfaces are still hot enough to grab it, and scatter the parsley over. Serve within 10 minutes, because trapped steam softens the crust as they sit. Never cover the bowl with foil — that undoes an hour of work in three minutes.

tips: Beef tallow or duck fat gives a deeper, savorier crust than olive oil and holds up better at 450°F (230°C). Save the fat from a roast in a jar in the fridge for exactly this.
Make ahead: parboil, rough up, and refrigerate uncovered on a tray for up to 24 hours. The extra drying time in the fridge actually improves the crust.
If the potatoes stick to the pan, they were flipped too early. Give them another 5 minutes and they will release themselves once the crust sets.
Do not skip the baking soda but do not double it either — too much makes the potatoes taste faintly soapy and turns the exterior slimy.
A nonstick or thin sheet pan will not do this. Use heavy aluminum or steel so the pan holds its heat when cold potatoes land on it.
recipes.keyTemp: Roast at 450°F (230°C); the potatoes are done when the interior reads about 210°F (99°C) and the outside is deep brown and audibly hard when tapped.
recipes.pairing: Made for roast beef, a Sunday chicken, or a fried egg at midnight — with a cold beer.

recipes.title: Scalloped Potatoes with Gruyere
recipes.blurb: Paper-thin potatoes simmered in garlicky cream, layered up, and baked until the top is bronzed and the middle is one tender, sliceable thing. It is the dish people ask you to bring.

items: 3 lb (1.35 kg) russet potatoes, peeled and sliced 1/8 in (3 mm) thick
1 tbsp (14 g) unsalted butter, softened, for the dish
6 oz (170 g) Gruyere cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 1/2 cups)
1 oz (30 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated (about 1/2 cup)
1 tbsp (4 g) chopped fresh chives, for serving

instructions.title: Heat the oven and butter the dish
instructions.text: Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat to 375°F (190°C). Rub a 9 x 13-inch (23 x 33 cm) baking dish generously with the softened butter, corners included. The butter is not just for sticking — it helps the edges of the potatoes brown and gives the finished gratin a cleaner release.

instructions.title: Slice the potatoes thin
instructions.text: Slice the peeled russets 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, using a mandoline if you have one and the guard that came with it. Consistent thickness is the whole game: thick slices stay chalky in the middle while thin ones dissolve. If you are knife-slicing, cut a thin sliver off one side first so each potato sits flat and cannot roll.

instructions.title: Do not rinse them
instructions.text: Resist every instinct to rinse the slices in water. The surface starch is exactly what thickens the cream into a sauce that sets, and washing it away gives you a soupy gratin that runs across the plate. If you sliced ahead, hold them in a bowl and cover with a damp towel rather than water.

instructions.title: Build the cream
instructions.text: In a wide pot or deep skillet, combine the heavy cream, whole milk, minced garlic, thyme sprigs, bay leaves, 2 teaspoons salt, black pepper, and nutmeg. Bring to a bare simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally, about 5 minutes. You are steeping flavor into the dairy — it should smell strongly of garlic and thyme before the potatoes go anywhere near it.

instructions.title: Simmer the slices in the cream
instructions.text: Slide the potato slices into the hot cream, separating any that are stuck together, and bring back to a gentle simmer. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring gently with a rubber spatula every couple of minutes so the bottom does not scorch. The cream will visibly thicken and coat the back of a spoon as starch leaches out, and the slices will bend without snapping.

instructions.title: Fish out the woody bits
instructions.text: Pull out the bay leaves and any bare thyme stems with tongs and discard them. Taste a slice of potato and a spoonful of the cream — it should taste slightly saltier than you want the finished dish to be, because the potatoes will keep absorbing seasoning in the oven. Adjust with another 1/4 teaspoon salt if it tastes flat.

instructions.title: Layer half into the dish
instructions.text: Spoon about half the potatoes into the buttered dish and use the back of a spoon to press them into a flat, even layer with no big air pockets. Pour over enough of the cream to just cover them. Flat layers are what let you cut clean squares later instead of serving spoonfuls of rubble.

instructions.title: Cheese the middle
instructions.text: Scatter half the Gruyere evenly over the first layer, right out to the edges. Cheese in the middle keeps the interior rich and gives you that pull when you lift a portion. Save the Parmigiano entirely for the top — it browns better than Gruyere and gives you the crackly lid.

instructions.title: Finish the layers
instructions.text: Add the remaining potatoes, press flat again, and pour over all the remaining cream — it should come up just below the top layer, not drown it. Top with the rest of the Gruyere and all the Parmigiano. Wipe any drips off the rim so they do not carbonize and smoke.

instructions.title: Bake covered, then uncovered
instructions.text: Cover the dish tightly with foil, set it on a rimmed sheet pan to catch bubble-overs, and bake for 40 minutes. Remove the foil and bake another 30 to 35 minutes, until the top is deeply browned in patches and the cream is bubbling slowly around the edges. Covered time cooks the potatoes through; uncovered time builds the crust.

instructions.title: Test the center
instructions.text: Push a paring knife straight down through the middle of the dish — it should meet no resistance at all, sliding through like soft butter. An instant-read thermometer in the center should show at least 200°F (93°C). If the knife catches, tent with foil and give it another 10 to 15 minutes.

instructions.title: Rest before you cut
instructions.text: Let the gratin sit on a rack for a full 20 minutes before serving. The cream is still liquid the moment it leaves the oven and needs that time to set into something sliceable. Scatter the chives over just before serving, and cut squares with a thin knife rather than scooping.

tips: Russets have the most starch and give the best-setting sauce. Yukon Golds work and taste sweeter, but the result is a little looser — do not use waxy red potatoes at all.
Make ahead: assemble completely, cover, and refrigerate up to 24 hours. Add 15 minutes to the covered bake and start from cold, not room temperature.
Traditional scalloped potatoes have no cheese at all — leave both cheeses out and you have a classic potatoes dauphinoise, which is just as good with roast lamb.
If the top browns before the center is tender, lay foil loosely over it. Browning is a surface event and can always be paused; undercooked potatoes cannot be rescued at the table.
Leftovers reheat beautifully: cut a square, put it in a skillet with a teaspoon of butter over medium-low heat, and crisp both cut faces for 3 minutes each.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the center reads 200°F (93°C) and a knife slides through with zero resistance. Rest 20 minutes so the cream sets.
recipes.pairing: Ham, prime rib, or a roast leg of lamb — and a glass of dry Riesling to cut the cream.

recipes.title: Steakhouse Creamed Spinach
recipes.blurb: Thick, nutmeg-scented, and rich enough to eat with a spoon — the side dish that makes a steak dinner feel like an occasion. The secret is squeezing the spinach far drier than feels reasonable.

items: 2 lb (900 g) fresh spinach, stems removed (or 20 oz / 570 g frozen chopped spinach, thawed)
1 tbsp (18 g) kosher salt, for blanching
1 medium shallot (about 2 oz / 55 g), finely minced
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions.title: Set up a blanch and a shock
instructions.text: Bring 4 quarts (3.8 L) of water to a hard boil with 1 tablespoon (18 g) of salt, and fill a large bowl with ice and cold water next to the stove. Blanching then shocking locks in the bright green color instead of letting the spinach go army-drab. Have a colander in the sink ready to go, because this part moves fast.

instructions.title: Blanch the spinach fast
instructions.text: Push the spinach into the boiling water in two batches and cook each for just 30 to 45 seconds, pressing it under with tongs. It will collapse to a fraction of its volume almost immediately. Longer than a minute and you cook out both the color and the flavor, leaving you with nothing but the cream.

instructions.title: Shock and drain
instructions.text: Lift the spinach straight into the ice water and swish it around for 30 seconds until it is cold to the touch. Stopping the cooking cold is the difference between vivid green and dull olive. Drain it in the colander and press down with your palm to push out the first round of water.

instructions.title: Squeeze it truly dry
instructions.text: Gather the spinach in a clean kitchen towel, twist the ends in opposite directions, and wring hard over the sink. You should get out at least 1 cup (240 ml) of green water, and the ball left in the towel should be dense and about the size of a large orange. Every tablespoon of water you leave behind will thin the sauce into soup.

instructions.title: Chop the ball
instructions.text: Unwrap the squeezed spinach and chop it roughly, running your knife through the compressed mass 15 or 20 times. It will be tightly packed and want to stay in a puck, so pull it apart with your fingers as you go. Loose, chopped spinach folds into the sauce evenly instead of arriving in solid clumps.

instructions.title: Sweat the aromatics
instructions.text: Melt the 4 tablespoons (55 g) butter in a 10-inch (25 cm) skillet over medium heat, then add the shallot with a pinch of salt. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it is soft and translucent but has taken on no color at all. Add the garlic and cook 45 seconds more, just until it smells sweet rather than raw.

instructions.title: Cook out the flour
instructions.text: Sprinkle the 1/4 cup (30 g) flour over the butter and whisk constantly for 90 seconds to 2 minutes. The paste will look sandy, then smooth, and will smell faintly like toasted pie crust. That smell means the raw flour taste is gone, which is the difference between a real bechamel and a chalky white sauce.

instructions.title: Build the bechamel
instructions.text: Pour in the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of warm milk in a thin stream while whisking hard, adding about 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time and letting each addition come together before the next. Adding it all at once makes lumps that no amount of whisking fully undoes. Once it is all in, stir in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) of heavy cream and bring to a gentle simmer. Two cups of liquid against 1/4 cup of flour is the ratio you want here — a thinner sauce will slide off the spinach and pool in the bowl.

instructions.title: Thicken and season
instructions.text: Simmer for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring often and scraping the corners of the pan, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon and holds a line when you drag a finger through it. Stir in the nutmeg, 1 teaspoon salt, and the black pepper. Make it slightly over-seasoned now, because 2 pounds of spinach is about to dilute it.

instructions.title: Fold and finish
instructions.text: Add the chopped spinach and stir until every strand is coated, then cook 2 to 3 minutes more to heat it through. Kill the heat and stir in the Parmigiano until it melts smoothly — off the heat so it does not break into greasy strings. Taste, add salt in 1/4 teaspoon increments, and serve hot in a warm bowl.

tips: Frozen chopped spinach works genuinely well here and saves 15 minutes. Thaw it fully and squeeze it just as ruthlessly — 20 oz (570 g) frozen equals about 2 lb (900 g) fresh.
Make ahead: the whole thing holds in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently over low heat with a splash of milk, stirring, because high heat will break the sauce.
If your sauce is thin, it is almost always wet spinach, not a bad roux. Simmer uncovered for a few extra minutes and it will tighten back up.
Grate the nutmeg fresh if you possibly can. Pre-ground nutmeg has lost most of its aroma, and nutmeg is the flavor that makes this taste like a steakhouse.
For a bit of tang, swap 2 oz (55 g) of the Parmigiano for cream cheese stirred in off the heat.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature to chase — the sauce is ready when it coats a spoon and holds a clean line under your finger. Serve hot, above 150°F (66°C).
recipes.pairing: Non-negotiable next to a ribeye, but just as good with roast chicken or spooned over a baked potato.

recipes.title: Balsamic Roasted Brussels Sprouts
recipes.blurb: Roasted hard until the cut faces are almost burnt and the loose leaves turn to chips, then glossed with a sweet-sharp balsamic glaze. This is the recipe that converts people who swear they hate sprouts.

items: 2 lb (900 g) Brussels sprouts, trimmed and halved through the stem
1/4 cup (25 g) shaved Parmigiano-Reggiano, for serving

instructions.title: Get the oven properly hot
instructions.text: Set a rack in the lower third of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C), sliding a heavy rimmed sheet pan in to preheat with it. A hot pan sears the cut faces on contact instead of letting the sprouts slowly steam in their own moisture. The lower rack puts them closer to the heat source for better browning underneath.

instructions.title: Trim and halve
instructions.text: Cut a thin slice off the dry stem end of each sprout and pull off any yellowed or loose outer leaves. Halve each one straight through the stem so both halves stay held together. Halving is what gives you the flat face that browns — whole sprouts steam and stay bitter in the middle.

instructions.title: Keep the stray leaves
instructions.text: Collect all the leaves that fell off during trimming and add them to the bowl with the sprouts. They roast into crisp, dark green chips that are the best part of the pan. Anyone who tells you to throw them away has never eaten one.

instructions.title: Toss with oil and salt
instructions.text: Toss the halved sprouts and loose leaves with the 3 tablespoons (45 ml) olive oil, 1 teaspoon salt, and the pepper until every surface is lightly slicked. Dry patches will not brown, and puddles of oil will fry rather than roast. Use your hands so you can feel when the coating is even.

instructions.title: Lay them cut side down
instructions.text: Pull the hot pan out and quickly arrange the sprouts cut side down in a single layer, giving each one a little space. You should hear an immediate sizzle when they land. Taking two extra minutes to turn them all face-down is the single biggest thing you can do for the final result.

instructions.title: Roast without stirring
instructions.text: Roast for 18 minutes without touching or shaking the pan. That uninterrupted contact between the cut face and the hot metal is where the deep caramelization happens, and stirring at minute 10 resets the whole process. The kitchen should smell nutty and sweet, not sulfurous.

instructions.title: Check and finish roasting
instructions.text: Lift one sprout with tongs — the cut face should be deep mahogany brown with some near-black edges, and the sprout should give easily when squeezed. If it is still pale, give it 4 to 7 more minutes. Total roasting time runs 22 to 28 minutes depending on the size of your sprouts.

instructions.title: Reduce the balsamic
instructions.text: While the sprouts roast, simmer the balsamic vinegar and honey in a small saucepan over medium heat for 4 to 6 minutes, until it has reduced by about half and coats a spoon in a thin syrup. Watch it closely at the end — balsamic goes from glaze to tar in under a minute. Pull it off the heat and whisk in the butter and the red pepper flakes.

instructions.title: Toss, shave, serve
instructions.text: Tip the hot sprouts into a serving bowl, drizzle over the warm glaze, and toss just enough to coat — dressing them on the pan makes the crisp faces go soggy against the metal. Shave the Parmigiano over the top with a vegetable peeler. Serve right away, while the edges are still crunchy.

tips: Buy sprouts of similar size, and if some are much bigger, quarter those instead of halving so everything finishes at the same moment.
Make ahead: trim and halve up to 3 days early and keep them in a bag in the fridge. Do not oil them until roasting day.
For a smoky version, cook 4 oz (115 g) chopped bacon on the pan for 10 minutes first, then roast the sprouts in the rendered fat and skip the olive oil.
Bitterness means undercooked, not bad sprouts. Push them further into the brown than you think is right and the bitterness turns into sweetness.
If you would rather skip reducing the balsamic, a good store-bought balsamic glaze drizzled over works fine — use about 3 tablespoons (45 ml).
recipes.keyTemp: Roast at 425°F (220°C). Done when the cut faces are deep brown to nearly black at the edges and a knife slips into the core with no resistance.
recipes.pairing: Great alongside pork chops, roast chicken, or a holiday ham — try a glass of Pinot Noir.

recipes.title: Garlic Parmesan Roasted Asparagus
recipes.blurb: Fifteen minutes from bunch to table, with tips that go crisp and a lemony parmesan crust. This is the side dish for nights when dinner is already almost done.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) asparagus, medium thickness (about 2 bunches)
1 tsp finely grated lemon zest, plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) juice
1 tbsp (14 g) unsalted butter, cut into small bits

instructions.title: Heat the oven high
instructions.text: Set a rack in the upper third of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C). Asparagus is mostly water and needs high, dry heat to brown before it collapses. A moderate oven at 350°F (175°C) will only ever steam it into something limp and gray-green.

instructions.title: Snap or cut the ends
instructions.text: Hold a spear near the bottom and bend it until it snaps — it breaks naturally right where the woody part ends, usually 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5 cm) up. Line up the rest of the bunch and cut them all at that same point with a knife. Woody ends stay stringy no matter how long you cook them.

instructions.title: Dry the spears
instructions.text: Rinse the asparagus and roll it in a clean kitchen towel until the spears are completely dry to the touch. Wet asparagus steams itself on the pan and never browns. This takes 30 seconds and changes the outcome more than any seasoning will.

instructions.title: Dress on the pan
instructions.text: Spread the spears on a rimmed sheet pan, drizzle with the 2 tablespoons (30 ml) olive oil, and roll them around with your hands until each one is glossy. Sprinkle over the 3/4 teaspoon salt and the pepper. Hold the garlic back for now — minced garlic burns and turns acrid in a 425°F (220°C) oven over a full 15 minutes.

instructions.title: Give them room
instructions.text: Arrange the spears in a single layer with a little space between them, all pointing the same direction so they are easy to turn later. Piled asparagus traps steam and comes out soft and drab. Use two pans rather than crowding one.

instructions.title: Roast until just tender
instructions.text: Roast for 8 to 10 minutes for medium spears, or 6 minutes for pencil-thin ones. They are ready when the color has gone bright, glossy green and a knife tip meets a little resistance at the thickest part. Overcooked asparagus goes limp and khaki and cannot be undone.

instructions.title: Add garlic and cheese
instructions.text: Pull the pan out, scatter the minced garlic and the 1/2 cup (50 g) Parmigiano over the spears, and dot the butter bits between them. Slide the pan back in for 3 to 5 minutes, until the cheese has melted into lacy golden patches and the garlic smells sweet. Watch it — the cheese goes from golden to bitter in about 60 seconds.

instructions.title: Finish with lemon
instructions.text: Transfer the spears to a warm platter, scraping every crispy cheese shard off the pan with a spatula, and squeeze over the 1 tablespoon (15 ml) lemon juice. Shower with the lemon zest. The acid at the very end wakes the whole thing up, and adding it before roasting would only dull the color.

tips: Thickness matters more than the recipe: pencil-thin spears need 6 to 8 minutes total, thick ones need 12 to 14. Judge by the knife, not the clock.
Store asparagus like flowers — standing in an inch of water in a jar in the fridge, loosely bagged. It stays crisp for 4 or 5 days instead of two.
Grate the cheese yourself. Pre-shredded parmesan is coated with anti-caking starch and refuses to melt into that lacy crust.
This works just as well on a hot grill: 4 to 6 minutes turning once, then toss with the garlic, cheese, and lemon off the heat.
Leftovers are excellent chopped cold into a frittata or scattered over pasta the next day.
recipes.keyTemp: Roast at 425°F (220°C). Done when the spears are bright green, a knife tip meets slight resistance at the base, and the cheese is golden and lacy.
recipes.pairing: Perfect next to salmon, steak, or a spring roast lamb — pour a crisp Sauvignon Blanc.

recipes.title: Buttermilk Skillet Cornbread
recipes.blurb: Poured into a screaming hot buttered cast iron pan so the crust fries as it bakes. Crunchy edges, tender crumb, and a wedge that begs for butter and honey.

items: 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) buttermilk, at room temperature
Flaky salt, about 1/4 tsp, for serving

instructions.title: Preheat the oven and the skillet
instructions.text: Set a rack in the center of the oven, put a 10-inch (25 cm) cast iron skillet on it, and heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Let the skillet sit in there for a full 15 minutes after the oven beeps. A truly hot pan is what fries the outside of the batter into that crunchy shell the second it hits.

instructions.title: Whisk the dry ingredients
instructions.text: In a large bowl, whisk together the cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and 1 1/4 teaspoons salt for 20 seconds. Whisking distributes the leaveners evenly, and a clump of baking soda tastes like metal and leaves a green streak. Make a well in the center.

instructions.title: Melt and split the butter
instructions.text: Melt all 6 tablespoons (85 g) of butter in a small saucepan or the microwave. Set 2 tablespoons (28 g) aside for the skillet and let the remaining 4 tablespoons (55 g) cool for 2 minutes. Pouring hot butter straight into eggs scrambles them, which is a mistake you only make once.

instructions.title: Mix the wet ingredients
instructions.text: In a second bowl, whisk the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) buttermilk and the 2 eggs until uniformly pale yellow with no streaks of white, about 30 seconds. Whisk in the 4 tablespoons (55 g) of cooled melted butter. Room-temperature buttermilk matters here — cold buttermilk will resolidify the butter into little flecks. Do not be tempted to add more buttermilk: this much liquid against 210 g of cornmeal is what gives you a batter that domes instead of one that bakes into pudding.

instructions.title: Combine with restraint
instructions.text: Pour the wet into the dry and fold with a spatula just until no dry pockets remain, about 15 strokes. The batter should look slightly lumpy and pourable, like thick pancake batter. Overmixing develops gluten in the flour and gives you cornbread with a tight, rubbery crumb.

instructions.title: Let it hydrate
instructions.text: Let the batter stand for 5 minutes while the skillet finishes heating. The cornmeal absorbs liquid and softens in that time, which is the difference between a tender crumb and a gritty one. You will see the batter thicken noticeably.

instructions.title: Butter the hot pan
instructions.text: Pull the skillet out with a dry oven mitt, set it on the stovetop, and swirl in the reserved 2 tablespoons (28 g) of butter. It should foam and sizzle instantly and start smelling nutty within about 15 seconds. Tilt the pan so the butter climbs the sides — that is where the crispy rim comes from.

instructions.title: Pour and level
instructions.text: Pour all the batter into the center of the hot skillet in one go; it should hiss loudly and the edges should begin setting immediately. Give the pan a quick shake to level the surface rather than spreading it with a spatula. Get it back into the oven within 30 seconds so the pan does not lose heat.

instructions.title: Bake until domed and golden
instructions.text: Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the top is golden brown, the center is domed and springs back when you press it, and the edges have pulled slightly from the pan. A toothpick in the center should come out with a few dry crumbs and no wet batter. The internal temperature should read 200°F (93°C).

instructions.title: Rest, then serve warm
instructions.text: Let the cornbread rest in the skillet on a rack for 10 minutes so the crumb sets and the steam redistributes. Cut into 8 wedges right in the pan and serve warm with the honey and a pinch of flaky salt. Cornbread is best within an hour of baking — it stales faster than any other quick bread.

tips: No buttermilk? Stir 1 1/2 tablespoons (22 ml) of lemon juice or white vinegar into 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of whole milk and let it sit 10 minutes until it curdles.
Southern-style is barely sweet; Northern-style is cakier. Drop the sugar to 1 teaspoon for a savory pan, or raise it to 1/3 cup (65 g) for a sweeter one.
No cast iron? Use a 9-inch (23 cm) cake pan or a metal 8 x 8-inch (20 x 20 cm) pan, preheated the same way. Glass or ceramic will not give you the crust.
Fold in 1 cup (170 g) of corn kernels, 4 oz (115 g) of grated sharp cheddar, or 2 minced jalapenos at the very end for a loaded version.
Day-old cornbread makes the best stuffing and the best croutons — cube it, toast at 300°F (150°C) for 20 minutes, and keep it in a bag.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 450°F (230°C) until the center reads 200°F (93°C) and springs back when pressed. Rest 10 minutes before cutting.
recipes.pairing: Chili, pulled pork, or a pot of collards — with a cold glass of buttermilk or a lager.

recipes.title: Soft Buttery Dinner Rolls
recipes.blurb: Cloud-soft, pull-apart rolls with a shiny golden top and a slick of butter brushed on the second they leave the oven. Nothing you buy comes close to these.

items: 4 cups (500 g) bread flour, plus more for dusting
1 cup (240 ml) whole milk, warmed to 105-110°F (40-43°C)
6 tbsp (85 g) unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp (15 ml) water, for the egg wash
3 tbsp (42 g) unsalted butter, melted, for brushing
1 tsp neutral oil, for the rising bowl

instructions.title: Warm the milk correctly
instructions.text: Heat the milk to 105 to 110°F (40 to 43°C) — warm on your wrist like bathwater, never hot. Above about 130°F (54°C) you start killing the yeast, and below 90°F (32°C) it works so slowly your rise will take all afternoon. If you have a thermometer, this is a good moment to use it.

instructions.title: Mix the dough base
instructions.text: In the bowl of a stand mixer, whisk together the bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Add the warm milk and the room-temperature egg, and mix on low with the dough hook for 2 minutes until a shaggy mass forms with no dry flour at the bottom. Let it rest 5 minutes — this autolyse hydrates the flour and makes the kneading much easier.

instructions.title: Add the butter slowly
instructions.text: With the mixer on medium-low, add the 6 tablespoons (85 g) of softened butter one tablespoon at a time, waiting until each piece disappears before adding the next. This takes about 5 minutes and looks alarming — the dough will break apart and slap around before it comes back together. Adding all the butter at once coats the flour and prevents gluten from ever forming.

instructions.title: Knead to the windowpane
instructions.text: Knead on medium for 8 to 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth, glossy, and pulls cleanly away from the sides while still sticking slightly at the bottom. Test it by stretching a walnut-sized piece between your fingers — it should thin to a translucent membrane before tearing. If it tears immediately, knead 3 more minutes and test again.

instructions.title: First rise
instructions.text: Oil a large bowl with the 1 teaspoon of neutral oil, turn the dough in it to coat, and cover with plastic wrap. Let it rise in a warm spot, around 75 to 78°F (24 to 26°C), for 60 to 90 minutes, until doubled. Judge by size, not the clock — press two fingers 1/2 inch (1 cm) into the dough and it is ready if the dent fills back only halfway.

instructions.title: Divide by weight
instructions.text: Punch the dough down gently and turn it onto a lightly floured counter. Weigh the whole mass — it should come to around 2 lb 1 oz (940 g) — then divide by 15 and cut equal pieces of about 2 1/4 oz (62 g) each. Equal weights mean equal baking times, and eyeballing it always leaves you with two burnt rolls and two doughy ones. Use the scale even if you never use it for anything else.

instructions.title: Shape tight balls
instructions.text: Flatten each piece, fold the edges into the center to make a rough ball, then flip it seam-side down and cup your palm over it, dragging it in small circles against the counter. The surface should tighten into a smooth, taut skin over about 10 seconds. That tension is what makes the roll rise up instead of spreading out.

instructions.title: Arrange in the pan
instructions.text: Butter a 9 x 13-inch (23 x 33 cm) baking pan and set the rolls in it in 3 rows of 5, leaving about 1/2 inch (1 cm) between them. They will grow into each other and give you soft pull-apart sides. If you want crustier rolls all round, space them further apart on a sheet pan instead.

instructions.title: Second rise
instructions.text: Cover loosely with plastic wrap or a damp towel and let rise 45 to 60 minutes at room temperature, until the rolls are puffy, touching each other, and look about 1 1/2 times their original size. Poke one gently — the dent should spring back slowly. Underproofed rolls burst open at the sides in the oven; overproofed ones collapse.

instructions.title: Heat the oven and wash the tops
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) about 20 minutes before the second rise finishes. Brush the tops gently with the egg wash using a soft pastry brush, going lightly so you do not deflate them. The egg is what gives you that deep mahogany shine instead of a pale, matte top.

instructions.title: Bake until deeply golden
instructions.text: Bake on the center rack for 18 to 22 minutes, rotating the pan halfway through, until the tops are a rich golden brown and the sides feel firm. The center of a middle roll should register 190°F (88°C) on an instant-read thermometer. If the tops brown before that, tent loosely with foil and keep going.

instructions.title: Butter them hot
instructions.text: The moment the pan comes out, brush the tops generously with the 3 tablespoons (42 g) of melted butter and sprinkle with the flaky salt. Hot rolls drink the butter straight in instead of letting it sit on top. Let them cool in the pan for 10 minutes before pulling them apart.

instructions.title: Serve or store
instructions.text: Serve warm, straight from the pan, with more butter on the table. They are at their absolute best within 4 hours of baking. Store leftovers in a zip-top bag at room temperature for 2 days and refresh them 5 minutes in a 300°F (150°C) oven.

tips: Make ahead: after shaping, cover the pan and refrigerate overnight. In the morning let them sit at room temperature 60 to 90 minutes until puffy, then bake as written.
Bread flour gives the chew and structure these need. All-purpose works but produces a softer, more cake-like roll that tears rather than pulls.
If your kitchen is cold, proof the dough in the oven with only the light on — that pocket sits around 80°F (27°C), which is perfect.
Freeze baked rolls for up to 2 months. Thaw at room temperature, then warm 8 minutes at 325°F (165°C) and brush with butter again.
Active dry yeast works too — just dissolve it in the warm milk with a pinch of the sugar and wait 10 minutes for it to foam before mixing.
recipes.keyTemp: Milk for the yeast: 105-110°F (40-43°C). Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the center of a middle roll reads 190°F (88°C).
recipes.pairing: Any holiday table, any pot of soup — and honey butter alongside is never a mistake.

recipes.title: Caesar Salad with Real Dressing
recipes.blurb: A proper Caesar built from egg yolks, anchovies, and garlic, emulsified by hand until it clings to every leaf. Once you taste the real thing the bottled stuff stops existing.

items: 2 large egg yolks, from pasteurized eggs (see step 2), plus 1 extra yolk held in reserve in case the dressing breaks
2 garlic cloves, grated on a microplane
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
3/4 cup (180 ml) neutral oil, such as grapeseed
1 oz (30 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated (about 1/2 cup)
6 oz (170 g) day-old sourdough or country bread, torn into 1-inch (2.5 cm) pieces
3 romaine hearts (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g total), leaves separated
2 oz (55 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, shaved with a peeler
1/4 tsp flaky sea salt, for finishing

instructions.title: Toast the croutons
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Toss the torn bread with the 3 tablespoons (45 ml) olive oil and 1/2 teaspoon salt on a sheet pan and bake for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once, until deep golden and crisp on the outside but still slightly chewy at the center. Rub the cut garlic clove over the hot croutons the second they come out — the heat pulls the garlic oil right in.

instructions.title: Handle the raw yolks safely
instructions.text: A classic Caesar uses raw egg yolk, so buy pasteurized eggs if you can find them. If you cannot, coddle whole eggs by lowering them into boiling water for exactly 60 seconds and then into ice water — that kills surface bacteria without setting the yolk. Anyone pregnant, elderly, or immunocompromised should use pasteurized eggs only, or 3 tablespoons (45 ml) of good mayonnaise in place of the yolks.

instructions.title: Mash the anchovy paste
instructions.text: On a cutting board, chop the 4 anchovy fillets with the grated garlic and 1/4 teaspoon of the kosher salt, then drag the flat of your knife across the pile 10 or 12 times until it turns into a smooth gray paste. The salt acts as an abrasive here, which is why the paste comes together faster than it would with the knife alone. Anchovies are not optional and they will not taste fishy — they dissolve into pure savory depth. Left in chunks, though, you get a nasty bite of raw fish in one forkful.

instructions.title: Build the emulsion base
instructions.text: In a medium bowl, whisk the egg yolks, anchovy-garlic paste, Dijon, lemon juice, and Worcestershire until completely smooth and pale, about 30 seconds. Set the bowl on a damp folded towel so it cannot spin while you whisk one-handed. Both the yolks and the mustard are emulsifiers, and this base is what will hold a full cup of oil.

instructions.title: Add the oil drop by drop
instructions.text: Start whisking constantly and add the neutral oil literally a few drops at a time for the first 2 tablespoons (30 ml). You will feel the mixture stiffen and turn glossy as the emulsion takes hold. This slow start is the entire difference between mayonnaise and a broken puddle of oil and egg.

instructions.title: Speed up and finish the oil
instructions.text: Once it has visibly thickened, pour the rest of the neutral oil in a thin, steady stream while whisking, then do the same with the olive oil. The dressing should end up thick enough to coat a spoon heavily and hold soft peaks. All the olive oil at once would make it bitter, which is why it goes in last and in a smaller amount.

instructions.title: Rescue a broken dressing
instructions.text: If it splits into a greasy, curdled mess — usually because the oil went in too fast at the start — do not throw it out, because every bit of that flavor is still in the bowl. Put the reserve egg yolk in a clean bowl with 1 teaspoon of warm water, whisk it smooth, then whisk the broken mixture into it a teaspoon at a time exactly the way you began. The fresh yolk gives the oil something to grab onto again. It comes back together every time, and nobody will ever know.

instructions.title: Cheese and season
instructions.text: Whisk in the 1 oz (30 g) of finely grated Parmigiano, the remaining 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt, and the 1/2 teaspoon black pepper. Taste on a lettuce leaf rather than a spoon, since a leaf tells you how it will actually eat. It should be aggressively sharp and salty — the romaine is going to mute it considerably. Anchovies and Parmigiano are both salty, so go a pinch at a time from here rather than a spoonful.

instructions.title: Prep and dry the romaine
instructions.text: Separate the leaves, wash them in cold water, and dry them thoroughly in a salad spinner or between towels. Water on the leaves is the number one reason Caesar salads turn watery and sad, because dressing slides off wet lettuce. Leave small inner leaves whole and tear the large outer ones into 3-inch (7.5 cm) pieces.

instructions.title: Chill the leaves
instructions.text: Put the dried leaves in a large bowl and refrigerate for at least 15 minutes, or up to 4 hours loosely covered. Cold, crisp romaine is what gives a Caesar its snap against the rich dressing. Room-temperature lettuce goes limp within a minute of being dressed.

instructions.title: Dress with a light hand
instructions.text: Add about two-thirds of the dressing to the cold leaves and toss with your hands, lifting from the bottom, until every leaf carries a thin sheen — not a puddle. Add more only if some leaves look dry. Over-dressed Caesar is heavy and slick; under-dressed can always be fixed at the table.

instructions.title: Plate and finish
instructions.text: Pile the leaves on chilled plates or a wide platter, tuck the croutons in among them rather than on top so they get a little dressing, and shave the 2 oz (55 g) of Parmigiano over with a vegetable peeler. Finish with the flaky salt and a few extra grinds of pepper. Serve immediately — a Caesar is a five-minute window.

tips: Make ahead: the dressing keeps 3 days covered in the fridge (2 days if using coddled rather than pasteurized eggs). It thickens when cold — whisk in a teaspoon of water to loosen it.
A food processor or immersion blender makes this nearly foolproof: blend everything but the oil, then drizzle the oil in with the motor running.
Day-old bread makes far better croutons than fresh. Fresh bread has too much moisture and steams into leathery cubes rather than crisping.
Buy anchovies packed in oil in a glass jar rather than a flat tin — they are usually meatier, and the leftovers keep in the fridge for a month.
For a grilled Caesar, halve the romaine hearts lengthwise, brush with oil, and grill cut side down over high heat for 90 seconds before dressing.
recipes.keyTemp: Use pasteurized eggs for raw yolks, or coddle whole eggs 60 seconds in boiling water. Keep the dressing and the salad below 40°F (4°C) until you serve.
recipes.pairing: A whole meal with grilled chicken or shrimp added, or the classic opener before steak — try a cold, dry Pinot Grigio.

recipes.title: Village-Style Greek Salad
recipes.blurb: No lettuce, big chunks, and a slab of feta laid over the top the way they do it in Greece. It takes twenty minutes and tastes like a hot afternoon by the water.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) ripe tomatoes, cut into 1-inch (2.5 cm) wedges
1 English cucumber (about 12 oz / 340 g), halved lengthwise and sliced 1/2 in (1 cm) thick
1/2 medium red onion (about 4 oz / 115 g), sliced paper thin
1 green bell pepper (about 6 oz / 170 g), seeded and cut into thin rings
1/2 cup (75 g) Kalamata olives, whole with pits
6 oz (170 g) block feta in brine, preferably Greek sheep's milk
1 pinch (about 1/8 tsp) flaky sea salt, for finishing

instructions.title: Buy the right tomatoes
instructions.text: This salad has nowhere to hide, so use the ripest tomatoes you can find — heirlooms, vine tomatoes, or big beefsteaks in summer. They should smell like tomato at the stem end and give slightly when squeezed. Out of season, cherry tomatoes halved are far better than pale winter slicers.

instructions.title: Never refrigerate the tomatoes
instructions.text: Keep tomatoes on the counter until you cut them, not in the fridge. Below about 55°F (13°C) the compounds that make tomatoes taste like tomatoes break down permanently and the flesh goes mealy. This is the single easiest upgrade to any tomato dish.

instructions.title: Cut in big chunks
instructions.text: Cut the tomatoes into generous 1-inch (2.5 cm) wedges and the cucumber into half-moons about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick. Greek village salad, horiatiki, is deliberately rustic — small dice turns everything to watery mush within minutes. Big pieces stay juicy and distinct.

instructions.title: Salt the tomatoes and wait
instructions.text: Put the tomato wedges in a colander set over a bowl, sprinkle with 1/2 teaspoon of the kosher salt, and let them sit 15 minutes. They will release a few tablespoons of intensely flavored juice, which seasons the tomatoes and stops the finished salad from flooding. Save that juice and whisk it into the dressing — it is free flavor.

instructions.title: Tame the raw onion
instructions.text: Slice the red onion as thin as you can manage, then soak the slices in a bowl of cold water for 10 minutes and drain well. This washes away the harsh sulfur compounds and leaves the sweetness and the crunch. Skip it and one aggressive onion slice can dominate the whole bowl.

instructions.title: Whisk the dressing
instructions.text: In a small bowl, whisk the olive oil, red wine vinegar, 1 teaspoon of the oregano, the black pepper, and any reserved tomato juice until it looks slightly cloudy and combined. The classic Greek ratio is about 4 parts oil to 1 part vinegar, which is gentler than a standard vinaigrette. Crush the dried oregano between your palms as you add it to wake up the oils.

instructions.title: Combine the vegetables
instructions.text: In a wide, shallow bowl, gently toss the drained tomatoes, cucumber, drained onion, pepper rings, and olives with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt. Use a folding motion rather than stirring so you do not bruise the tomatoes. The olives go in with their pits, which is traditional — just warn whoever you are feeding.

instructions.title: Dress and rest
instructions.text: Pour the dressing over and toss gently to coat, then let the salad stand 5 minutes at room temperature. That short rest lets the vinegar and oil find their way into the cucumber and pepper. Room temperature is important — cold mutes olive oil and dulls tomato flavor.

instructions.title: Lay the feta on top
instructions.text: Set the whole 6 oz (170 g) block of feta on top of the salad rather than crumbling it in. Drizzle it with a little olive oil from the bowl, sprinkle over the remaining 1/2 teaspoon oregano and the flaky salt. Everyone breaks off pieces with their fork, which is the whole point — crumbled feta dissolves into the dressing and disappears.

tips: Buy feta in brine, not the dry pre-crumbled kind. Greek sheep's milk feta is creamy and tangy; the crumbled tubs are drier, saltier, and usually made from cow's milk.
Serve with a piece of crusty bread and mop the bowl at the end. The oil and tomato juice left behind is considered the best part of the dish.
Make ahead: chop everything except the tomatoes up to a day early. Cut and salt the tomatoes and dress the salad no more than 30 minutes before eating.
Add 2 tablespoons (20 g) of capers, rinsed, or a handful of purslane if you find it — both are common in the Greek islands and both add a welcome sharpness.
If your olive oil tastes flat, it is old. Good extra-virgin should taste peppery at the back of the throat, and in a four-ingredient dressing you will notice.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking involved. Serve at cool room temperature, around 65°F (18°C) — colder than that and the olive oil turns waxy and the tomatoes taste like nothing.
recipes.pairing: Grilled lamb, chicken souvlaki, or just bread and a cold glass of Assyrtiko.

recipes.title: Creamy Buttermilk Coleslaw
recipes.blurb: Crunchy, tangy, and creamy without ever turning into a puddle, because the cabbage gets salted first. This is the slaw that belongs on a pulled pork sandwich.

items: 1 small green cabbage (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g), quartered and cored
1/4 small red cabbage (about 6 oz / 170 g), for color
2 medium carrots (about 6 oz / 170 g), peeled and coarsely grated
1 tbsp (18 g) kosher salt, for drawing out water
1/4 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
3 tbsp (10 g) chopped fresh chives or scallion greens

instructions.title: Shred the cabbage thin
instructions.text: Cut each cabbage quarter into thin ribbons about 1/8 inch (3 mm) wide, working from the cut side down so the wedge stays stable. A sharp chef's knife gives better texture than a food processor, which bruises and shreds unevenly. Thin ribbons hold dressing; thick chunks just push it around the bowl.

instructions.title: Salt and drain
instructions.text: Toss the shredded green and red cabbage with the 1 tablespoon (18 g) kosher salt in a colander set over a bowl and let it sit for 30 minutes at room temperature. You will see a surprising amount of liquid collect underneath — often 1/2 cup (120 ml) or more. This is the entire secret to slaw that stays crisp instead of turning watery in an hour.

instructions.title: Rinse the salt away
instructions.text: Rinse the cabbage thoroughly under cold running water for 30 seconds, tossing with your hands so the salt washes off every ribbon. Skipping this leaves you with a slaw so salty it is inedible. The cabbage has already given up its water, and rinsing will not put it back.

instructions.title: Dry it completely
instructions.text: Spin the rinsed cabbage in a salad spinner in batches, or gather it in a clean towel and wring it out over the sink. It should feel barely damp, not wet. Any water left clinging will thin the dressing into something runny within twenty minutes.

instructions.title: Grate the carrot
instructions.text: Grate the peeled carrots on the large holes of a box grater and add them to the dried cabbage. Do not salt the carrots — they are much lower in water and salting turns them limp. The carrot is for sweetness and color as much as for crunch.

instructions.title: Whisk the dressing
instructions.text: In a medium bowl, whisk the mayonnaise, buttermilk, cider vinegar, lemon juice, sugar, Dijon, celery seed, black pepper, and 1/4 teaspoon salt until completely smooth. It should be thick enough to coat a spoon but pourable. The buttermilk is what keeps this from tasting like straight mayonnaise.

instructions.title: Taste and balance
instructions.text: Taste the dressing on its own and adjust before it goes anywhere near the cabbage. It should taste noticeably sharper and sweeter than you want the final slaw to be, since the vegetables will mute it. Add vinegar 1 teaspoon at a time for sharpness, sugar 1 teaspoon at a time for balance.

instructions.title: Dress lightly at first
instructions.text: Pour about three-quarters of the dressing over the cabbage and carrots and toss with tongs until every strand is coated. Add the rest only if it looks dry. You can always add more dressing, but you cannot take it back out.

instructions.title: Chill to marry
instructions.text: Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour before serving. The flavors need that time to settle together, and the cabbage softens just slightly into the perfect texture. Straight from the bowl it tastes disjointed, like raw cabbage next to mayonnaise.

instructions.title: Refresh and serve cold
instructions.text: Just before serving, toss the slaw again to redistribute the dressing that has settled to the bottom, and taste for salt one last time. Stir in the chopped chives now so they stay bright green. Serve cold, below 40°F (4°C), and keep the bowl on ice if it is sitting out at a cookout.

tips: Make ahead: this is better on day two and keeps 4 days in the fridge. The pre-salting is what lets it survive that long without weeping.
For a vinegar slaw instead, skip the mayo and buttermilk and use 1/2 cup (120 ml) cider vinegar, 1/3 cup (80 ml) neutral oil, and 3 tablespoons (36 g) sugar.
A bagged coleslaw mix works in a pinch, but still salt and drain it. Bagged cabbage is often wetter than a whole head, not drier.
Celery seed is the flavor people cannot identify but always miss. It is worth buying a jar just for this and for potato salad.
Food safety at a picnic: mayonnaise-based slaw should not sit above 40°F (4°C) for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour if it is above 90°F (32°C) outside.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking. Serve and store cold, below 40°F (4°C); do not leave a mayonnaise dressing at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
recipes.pairing: Pulled pork, fried chicken, or a burger — and a cold cider or lemonade.

recipes.title: Honey Roasted Carrots with Thyme
recipes.blurb: Roasted until the edges caramelize, then tossed in a honey butter that turns them almost candy-sweet. Cheap, easy, and the first thing to disappear from the table.

items: 2 lb (900 g) carrots, peeled and cut on a bias into 2-inch (5 cm) pieces
1/4 tsp flaky sea salt, for finishing
2 tbsp (15 g) toasted chopped pistachios or walnuts, for serving

instructions.title: Heat the oven high
instructions.text: Set a rack in the upper third of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C). Carrots are full of sugar and need real heat to caramelize rather than just soften. A lower oven gives you sweet steamed carrots, which are fine but forgettable.

instructions.title: Cut on a bias
instructions.text: Peel the carrots and cut them on a strong diagonal into pieces about 2 inches (5 cm) long, halving the fat ends lengthwise so every piece is roughly the same thickness. Angled cuts expose far more surface area than straight rounds, and surface area is where browning happens. Uniform thickness is what keeps the thin ends from burning.

instructions.title: Dry and oil them
instructions.text: Pat the cut carrots dry with a towel, then toss them in a bowl with the 2 tablespoons (30 ml) olive oil, 1 teaspoon salt, and the pepper. Every surface should look barely glossy. Wet carrots steam themselves and stay pale no matter how hot the oven is.

instructions.title: Hold back the honey
instructions.text: Do not add the honey yet. Sugar burns at roasting temperatures long before carrots are tender, and honey added at the start turns black and bitter in about 15 minutes. It goes on at the very end, when the carrots are already cooked through.

instructions.title: Spread them out
instructions.text: Arrange the carrots in a single layer on a rimmed sheet pan with space between the pieces, cut sides down where you can manage it. Crowding traps steam and the carrots will never brown. If your pan looks full, split them across two pans.

instructions.title: Roast the first stretch
instructions.text: Roast for 20 minutes without stirring. The undersides need continuous contact with the hot pan to develop those dark caramelized patches. You should smell something distinctly sweet by about minute 15.

instructions.title: Flip and finish
instructions.text: Turn the carrots with a spatula and roast another 8 to 12 minutes, until they are deeply browned in places and a knife slides into the thickest piece with only slight resistance. They should be tender but still hold their shape when you lift them. Total time runs 28 to 32 minutes depending on thickness.

instructions.title: Make the honey butter
instructions.text: While the carrots finish, melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium-low heat, then whisk in the honey, lemon juice, and thyme leaves. Let it bubble gently for about 60 seconds until slightly thickened and glossy. The lemon keeps the honey from being cloying and the thyme keeps it from tasting like dessert.

instructions.title: Glaze and serve
instructions.text: Tip the hot carrots into a warm serving bowl, pour the honey butter over, and toss until every piece shines. Scatter the toasted nuts and the flaky salt on top. Serve within 10 minutes — the glaze is at its best while it is still loose and warm.

tips: Bagged baby carrots do not work well here. They are cut from larger carrots, hold extra water, and roast to a rubbery texture rather than caramelizing.
Make ahead: peel and cut the carrots up to 3 days early and store them in water in the fridge. Drain and dry them thoroughly before roasting.
Maple syrup works one-for-one in place of honey, and browns a little less aggressively if your oven runs hot.
For a savory version, swap the honey butter for 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of olive oil, 1 teaspoon of cumin, and a squeeze of lime.
If your carrots are old and bendy, soak them in ice water for 20 minutes first — they firm right back up and roast much better.
recipes.keyTemp: Roast at 425°F (220°C). Done when the edges are darkly caramelized and a knife meets only slight resistance in the thickest piece.
recipes.pairing: Roast chicken, pork loin, or a holiday ham — with a glass of off-dry Riesling.

recipes.title: Green Beans Almondine
recipes.blurb: Snappy blanched beans tossed in brown butter with toasted almonds and a hit of lemon. It is a fifty-year-old French restaurant classic and it still beats everything else on the table.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) green beans or haricots verts, ends trimmed
2 tbsp (36 g) kosher salt, for blanching
4 cups (about 500 g) ice, for the ice bath
1 medium shallot (about 2 oz / 55 g), thinly sliced
2 tbsp (30 ml) fresh lemon juice, plus 1 tsp grated zest
3/4 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions.title: Set up the blanch and shock
instructions.text: Bring 4 quarts (3.8 L) of water to a rolling boil with the 2 tablespoons (36 g) kosher salt, and fill a large bowl with ice and cold water right next to the stove. The water should taste like the sea — that is how the beans get seasoned all the way through. Having the ice bath ready before the beans go in is not optional, because you will need it within four minutes.

instructions.title: Trim only the stem ends
instructions.text: Line the beans up and cut off the tough stem ends in bunches, but leave the thin tapered tails on. Those tails are tender, they look beautiful on the plate, and trimming both ends is a habit worth breaking. Discard any beans that are limp or rusty at the ends.

instructions.title: Blanch until snappy
instructions.text: Drop the beans into the boiling water and cook for 3 to 4 minutes for standard green beans, or 2 minutes for thin haricots verts. Fish one out at 3 minutes and bite it — it should be bright green and squeaky with a little bite left, not soft. They will cook slightly more in the pan later, so pull them a touch early.

instructions.title: Shock them cold
instructions.text: Transfer the beans immediately into the ice water with a spider or tongs and swirl until they are cold all the way through, about 60 seconds. This stops the cooking on a dime and sets that vivid green color. Beans left to cool on their own keep cooking from residual heat and turn olive drab.

instructions.title: Dry them thoroughly
instructions.text: Drain the beans and spread them on a clean kitchen towel, then roll the towel up and pat them dry. Wet beans will hit the brown butter and spit violently, and the water will also loosen the sauce. At this point they can wait, refrigerated, for up to 2 days.

instructions.title: Toast the almonds in butter
instructions.text: Melt the 4 tablespoons (55 g) of butter in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium heat, then add the sliced almonds. Stir constantly for 3 to 4 minutes — the butter will foam, the foam will subside, and the almonds will turn golden. Never walk away from this; almonds go from perfect to burnt in about 30 seconds.

instructions.title: Brown the butter
instructions.text: Keep stirring as the milk solids at the bottom of the pan turn from pale to amber and the smell shifts from buttery to nutty and toasted, about 1 to 2 minutes more. Those browned milk solids are the entire flavor of the dish. If you see black flecks and smell anything acrid, start over — burnt butter cannot be saved.

instructions.title: Add the aromatics
instructions.text: Drop the heat to medium-low and add the sliced shallot and garlic. Cook for 90 seconds, stirring, until the shallot is soft and translucent and the garlic is fragrant but still pale. The lower heat stops the garlic from scorching in butter that is already very hot.

instructions.title: Toss the beans through
instructions.text: Add the dried beans along with the 3/4 teaspoon salt and the black pepper, and toss with tongs for 2 to 3 minutes until they are heated through and coated in butter and almonds. They should sizzle steadily, not smoke. Any longer and the beans go from snappy to soft.

instructions.title: Finish with lemon
instructions.text: Pull the pan off the heat and add the 2 tablespoons (30 ml) lemon juice and the zest, tossing to combine — it will sizzle and steam for a second. Off-heat acid keeps its brightness instead of cooking away. Taste, add salt in small pinches if needed, and serve straight from the pan while everything is hot.

tips: Make ahead: blanch, shock, and dry the beans up to 2 days early and keep them in a bag in the fridge. Then the whole dish is a 6-minute job at dinner.
Haricots verts are thinner and more tender than standard green beans and are worth the extra dollar. Just cut the blanching time to 2 minutes.
Buy sliced almonds, not slivered. Slivered almonds are too thick to toast evenly in a pan and stay hard against the tender beans.
Use a stainless or light-colored skillet so you can actually see the butter change color. In a black cast iron pan you are browning butter blind.
For a richer version, add 2 oz (55 g) of chopped bacon or pancetta at the start and use only 2 tablespoons (28 g) of butter.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature to hit. The beans are right when they are bright green and still snap slightly; the butter is right at amber with a nutty smell, around 250°F (120°C).
recipes.pairing: The classic partner to roast chicken, turkey, or a piece of sole — with a glass of white Burgundy.

recipes.title: Cauliflower Gratin with Mornay
recipes.blurb: Tender cauliflower under a proper Gruyere cheese sauce with a crunchy panko lid. It is macaroni and cheese in vegetable form, and nobody at the table will complain.

items: 2 medium heads cauliflower (about 3 lb / 1.35 kg total), cut into 1 1/2-inch (4 cm) florets
2 tbsp (36 g) kosher salt, for blanching
1 tbsp (14 g) unsalted butter, softened, for the dish
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
6 oz (170 g) Gruyere cheese, grated (about 1 1/2 cups)
2 oz (55 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated (about 1 cup)

instructions.title: Heat the oven and prep the dish
instructions.text: Set a rack in the upper-middle of the oven and heat to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9 x 13-inch (23 x 33 cm) baking dish or a 3-quart (2.8 L) gratin dish with the softened butter. A wide, shallow dish gives you more browned top per serving, which is the point of a gratin.

instructions.title: Cut even florets
instructions.text: Break the cauliflower into florets about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across, cutting through the stems rather than tearing so they stay intact. Trim the tough core but keep the tender inner stems — they are sweet and cook at the same rate as the florets. Even sizing means everything is tender at the same moment.

instructions.title: Blanch the cauliflower
instructions.text: Bring 4 quarts (3.8 L) of water to a boil with the 2 tablespoons (36 g) salt and cook the florets for 4 to 5 minutes, until a knife enters with slight resistance. You want them about 80 percent cooked, since they will finish in the oven. Raw cauliflower baked in sauce releases water and gives you a soupy gratin.

instructions.title: Drain and dry very well
instructions.text: Drain the florets in a colander and let them steam dry for a full 5 minutes, shaking once or twice, then blot the tops with a towel. Every drop of water still clinging will thin your sauce in the oven. This is the step people skip and then wonder why the gratin is watery.

instructions.title: Start the roux
instructions.text: Melt the 4 tablespoons (55 g) butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat until it foams. Whisk in the 1/4 cup (30 g) flour and cook, whisking constantly, for 90 seconds to 2 minutes. It will smell faintly like toast and turn a shade blonder — that is the raw flour taste cooking off.

instructions.title: Build the bechamel
instructions.text: Add the warm milk about 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time, whisking hard until each addition is fully smooth before you add the next. Warm milk and gradual addition are the two things that prevent lumps. Once all the milk is in, the sauce should be smooth and pourable.

instructions.title: Thicken and season
instructions.text: Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer and cook 4 to 5 minutes, whisking often and scraping the corners, until it thickly coats a spoon. Whisk in the Dijon, nutmeg, 1 teaspoon salt, and the black pepper. Taste it — it should be assertive, because a pile of cauliflower is about to dilute it.

instructions.title: Melt the cheese off the heat
instructions.text: Pull the pan completely off the burner and let it sit 60 seconds, then add the Gruyere and half the Parmigiano in three handfuls, stirring until each melts. Cheese added over direct heat overheats, the proteins tighten, and the sauce turns grainy and greasy. Off the heat it stays glossy and smooth.

instructions.title: Combine and fill the dish
instructions.text: Fold the dried cauliflower into the sauce until every floret is coated, then transfer everything to the buttered dish and spread it into an even layer. Nudge the florets so they sit snugly rather than in a mound. Even depth means even baking.

instructions.title: Make the crunchy topping
instructions.text: Toss the panko with the 2 tablespoons (28 g) melted butter, the remaining Parmigiano, the parsley, and 1/4 teaspoon salt until the crumbs look evenly damp. Scatter it over the gratin in a thin, even layer. Buttered crumbs fry as they bake, which is what makes them crunch instead of going soggy.

instructions.title: Bake until bubbling
instructions.text: Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until the sauce is bubbling slowly at the edges and the topping is golden brown. The center should register at least 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. If the top is pale but the sauce is bubbling, run it under the broiler for 60 to 90 seconds, watching the whole time.

instructions.title: Rest before serving
instructions.text: Let the gratin sit on a rack for 10 minutes before you serve it. The sauce is thin straight out of the oven and needs that time to set enough to spoon cleanly. Serve hot, scooping down to the bottom so everyone gets both crust and sauce.

tips: Grate your own Gruyere. Pre-shredded cheese is dusted with cellulose to keep it from clumping, and that starch makes a Mornay sauce gritty.
Make ahead: assemble everything except the panko topping up to 24 hours early and refrigerate. Add the topping just before baking and add 10 to 15 minutes from cold.
Swap in broccoli, romanesco, or a mix — the blanching time stays about the same for florets of the same size.
If the sauce breaks and goes greasy, whisk in 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of cold milk off the heat. It usually pulls back together.
For a sharper gratin, replace 2 oz (55 g) of the Gruyere with aged white cheddar. Do not use mozzarella, which turns stringy and bland in a Mornay.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the center reads at least 165°F (74°C) and the edges bubble. Rest 10 minutes so the sauce sets.
recipes.pairing: Roast beef, ham, or a big green salad if it is the main event — with a glass of dry Alsatian white.

recipes.title: Crispy Buttery Garlic Bread
recipes.blurb: Crunchy on top, soft underneath, and loaded with enough garlic butter to soak through. Twenty-five minutes and it makes any pasta night feel like a restaurant.

items: 1 loaf (16 oz / 450 g) Italian bread or ciabatta, split lengthwise
10 tbsp (140 g) unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
6 garlic cloves, finely grated on a microplane
1 extra garlic clove, halved, for rubbing
1/4 cup (15 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley

instructions.title: Heat the oven
instructions.text: Set a rack in the upper-middle of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C). A hot oven crisps the cut surface quickly, before the interior of the loaf dries out and turns to toast all the way through. Have a rimmed sheet pan ready but do not preheat it.

instructions.title: Split the loaf
instructions.text: Cut the loaf in half horizontally with a serrated knife, using a long sawing motion rather than pressing down so you do not crush the crumb. You want two long halves with as much flat cut surface as possible. That flat face is where all the butter goes.

instructions.title: Rub with raw garlic
instructions.text: Rub the cut faces all over with the halved garlic clove, pressing firmly so the rough surface of the bread grates the clove away. This layers a fresh, sharp garlic note underneath the mellow roasted garlic in the butter. It takes 20 seconds and it is the trick most recipes leave out.

instructions.title: Grate the garlic finely
instructions.text: Grate the 6 garlic cloves on a microplane into a bowl so they turn into a wet paste rather than pieces. Chopped garlic sits in chunks that scorch and turn bitter under a hot oven, while paste dissolves evenly through the butter. If you only have a knife, mince finely and then mash with a pinch of salt.

instructions.title: Make the garlic butter
instructions.text: Mash the softened butter with the garlic paste, half the Parmigiano, half the parsley, the 3/4 teaspoon salt, black pepper, and the red pepper flakes using a fork until it is a uniform, spreadable paste. The butter must be genuinely soft, around 65°F (18°C) — cold butter will not blend and melted butter will just run off the bread.

instructions.title: Spread it all the way out
instructions.text: Spread the garlic butter over both cut faces, going right to the crusts and into every hole in the crumb. Use all of it; it looks like too much and it is exactly the right amount. Bare edges are the parts that come out dry and disappointing.

instructions.title: Bake cut side up
instructions.text: Put the halves cut side up on the sheet pan and bake for 10 to 12 minutes, until the butter has fully melted into the bread and the edges are turning golden. The kitchen should smell strongly of garlic by minute 8. The bottom crust will crisp against the hot pan at the same time.

instructions.title: Broil for the finish
instructions.text: Scatter the remaining Parmigiano over the tops and slide the pan under the broiler for 1 to 2 minutes, until the surface is spotted deep golden brown and the cheese is bubbling. Do not walk away for even 30 seconds — broilers go from perfect to charcoal faster than anything else in the kitchen. Pull it when you see the first dark spots.

instructions.title: Cut and serve hot
instructions.text: Scatter the remaining parsley over, move the halves to a cutting board, and cut into 2-inch (5 cm) wide pieces with a serrated knife. Serve immediately, piled in a napkin-lined basket so the steam can escape. Covering it tightly softens the crust you just spent 15 minutes building.

tips: Make ahead: the garlic butter keeps 2 weeks in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer. Roll it in parchment into a log and slice off what you need.
You can assemble the buttered loaf, wrap it in foil, and freeze it. Bake from frozen at 425°F (220°C) for 20 minutes in the foil, then open it up and broil.
For soft, pull-apart garlic bread instead, wrap the buttered loaf in foil and bake 15 minutes at 350°F (175°C) without broiling.
Skip the pre-minced garlic in a jar. It is preserved in acid and tastes sour and metallic once it hits heat.
A dense, chewy loaf like ciabatta or a bakery Italian holds up best. Soft supermarket sub rolls collapse into a greasy sponge.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 425°F (220°C) then broil 1-2 minutes. It is done when the surface is spotted deep golden brown and the butter has soaked fully into the crumb.
recipes.pairing: Spaghetti and meatballs, lasagna, or a bowl of tomato soup — with a glass of Chianti.
