recipes.title: Buttery Rice Pilaf with Orzo
recipes.blurb: Toasted orzo and long-grain rice cooked in seasoned broth until every grain is separate and glossy. It is the boxed stuff you grew up on, except actually good.

items: 1 1/2 cups (280 g) long-grain white rice, such as basmati
1 small yellow onion (about 5 oz / 140 g), finely diced
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions.title: Rinse the rice
instructions.text: Put the rice in a fine-mesh sieve and rinse under cold running water, stirring with your fingers, until the water runs mostly clear — about 60 to 90 seconds. Rinsing washes away loose surface starch, which is what makes rice clump and turn sticky. Shake the sieve well and let it drain while you start the aromatics.

instructions.title: Sweat the onion
instructions.text: Melt the 3 tablespoons (42 g) butter with the olive oil in a heavy 3-quart (2.8 L) saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and a pinch of the salt and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent with no browning. The oil raises the smoke point so the butter does not scorch while the onion sweats.

instructions.title: Toast the orzo
instructions.text: Add the orzo and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes, until the little grains turn a nutty golden brown, like the color of a toasted almond. This toasting is what gives pilaf its distinctive flavor and keeps the pasta from going gluey. Watch closely — the pieces at the edge of the pan color first.

instructions.title: Toast the rice too
instructions.text: Add the drained rice and the minced garlic and stir for another 90 seconds to 2 minutes, until the grains look chalky and opaque rather than translucent, and smell faintly popcorn-like. Coating each grain in fat helps them stay separate in the finished pilaf. The garlic goes in now because a full two-minute toast would burn it.

instructions.title: Add the broth
instructions.text: Pour in the 3 1/4 cups (780 ml) of broth all at once, add the bay leaf, the remaining salt, and the black pepper, and stir once to loosen anything stuck to the bottom. It will steam and hiss loudly. The ratio here is a little over 1 1/2 parts liquid to 1 part grain, which is what 1 1/2 cups of rice plus 1/2 cup of dry orzo actually need — cut the broth back and the orzo comes out chalky in the middle. Scraping the bottom now matters too, because a stuck patch of orzo will scorch during the simmer.

instructions.title: Bring to a boil, then drop it
instructions.text: Raise the heat and bring the pot to a full boil, then immediately reduce to the lowest setting that keeps a bare simmer going. Cover with a tight-fitting lid. If your lid is loose, lay a sheet of foil across the pot before putting the lid on, since escaping steam means undercooked rice.

instructions.title: Simmer undisturbed
instructions.text: Cook, covered, for 18 minutes without lifting the lid or stirring even once. Every peek releases the steam that is doing the cooking, and stirring rubs starch loose and turns the pilaf into risotto. Trust the timer and walk away.

instructions.title: Rest off the heat
instructions.text: Take the pot off the burner and let it stand, still covered, for 10 full minutes. The rice continues to steam and the moisture redistributes from the wetter grains at the bottom to the drier ones on top. Skipping this rest is why home-cooked rice is so often soggy underneath and firm on top.

instructions.title: Fluff and enrich
instructions.text: Remove the lid and the bay leaf, dot the cold tablespoon (14 g) of butter over the surface, and fluff with a fork, lifting and separating rather than stirring. The grains should fall apart individually and look glossy. If you see any liquid at the bottom, leave the pot uncovered over low heat for 2 minutes.

instructions.title: Finish and serve
instructions.text: Fold in the parsley, lemon zest, and the toasted almonds if you are using them, and taste for salt — broth-cooked rice usually needs another 1/4 teaspoon. Serve hot, in a warm bowl. Pilaf holds well covered for about 20 minutes if dinner runs late.

tips: Broken vermicelli works in place of orzo and is the more traditional choice. Snap it into 1/2-inch (1 cm) pieces and toast it exactly the same way.
Make ahead: cook completely, cool, and refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat covered with 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of water in the microwave or a low oven.
Use low-sodium broth so you control the salt. Regular broth plus a teaspoon of salt will come out aggressively salty once it reduces into the rice.
If the rice is still firm after resting, add 3 tablespoons (45 ml) of hot water, cover, and give it 5 more minutes on the lowest heat.
For a richer pilaf, stir in 1/3 cup (50 g) of golden raisins with the broth and finish with toasted pine nuts instead of almonds.
recipes.keyTemp: Simmer covered on low for 18 minutes, then rest 10 minutes off the heat. Serve hot, above 140°F (60°C); cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.
recipes.pairing: Roast chicken, lamb kebabs, or anything with a pan sauce that needs somewhere to land.
